requirements.requirement: Provide an encrypted volume mounted at /srv/secure on node1
requirements.summary: A LUKS1-encrypted (aes-xts-plain64, 256-bit) file-backed volume was created via cryptsetup luksFormat/luksOpen, formatted ext4, and mounted at /srv/secure. Confirmed by mount/df/findmnt output and cryptsetup status showing 'active and is in use' with the /var/lib/secure/secure.img backing file.

requirements.requirement: Volume unlocks and mounts on its own at boot (no manual intervention)
requirements.summary: A custom systemd oneshot unit (secure-volume.service, enabled and Before=local-fs.target) invokes a keyfile-based luksOpen+mount helper script. This was validated end-to-end: pre-reboot baseline captured (boot_id, mount, cryptsetup, service state all healthy), a real reboot was triggered (shutdown -r now) and acknowledged, and post-reboot the boot_id changed, uptime reset to 0, and the service/mount/cryptsetup state came back healthy automatically without any manual unlock command being issued.

requirements.requirement: Data on the volume survives the boot cycle (durability of the encrypted store)
requirements.summary: A marker.txt file with a timestamp and md5 checksum was written before reboot; after reboot the same content and checksum were confirmed intact, and a new write succeeded, demonstrating full read/write functionality post-boot.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were directly and coherently demonstrated: an encrypted (LUKS1) volume was created and mounted at /srv/secure, a systemd oneshot unit was configured to auto-unlock (via keyfile) and auto-mount it before local-fs.target, and this was validated through a genuine, bounded reboot cycle showing a changed boot identity, automatic service activation, remounted volume, active LUKS mapping, and intact plus newly-written data. The provider-wide restart-evidence protocol coincides with the task's own required boot-cycle proof for node1 (the only managed node), and both align consistently with the fixed before/after-executor boot-identity snapshots. No unnecessary or unsafe mutations were found in the executor's command trace.
limitations: The keyfile enabling unattended unlock is stored on the same host filesystem (root-only, mode 400) rather than a network KMS or TPM-backed mechanism; this is a reasonable approach for boot-time automatic unlock without protecting against an attacker with root/disk access, but it does mean the volume is not protected against offline access to the underlying disk image plus keyfile — a note relevant to the intended threat model, not a task failure since the task only asked for volumes that unlock automatically at boot.

LUKS1 was used instead of LUKS2 due to cryptsetup 1.6.6 on this legacy Ubuntu 16.04 image; this is a platform constraint rather than an executor choice and does not affect satisfaction of the stated requirements.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command timeline reviewed chronologically: two initial commands (cmd-bb5041845bb8485c, cmd-3bb3c0197fc5422f) were read-only OS/version discovery. The main provisioning command (cmd-cd119361a68f4f1e) is a single bounded state-changing block directly building the required encrypted volume, helper script, and systemd unit — all retained artifacts have a clear causal role in satisfying the task. The pre-restart baseline capture (cmd-14243199fcb6435d) and reboot trigger (cmd-7d6962df2b504b18) are necessary for the restart-evidence protocol required by this task's own contract (boot-time auto-unlock). Post-reboot reconnection probes (cmd-e3e9168aae5542f2, cmd-3aff4408edd24063) are read-only. The final verification command (cmd-8041a745c17d428f) appends a small bounded line to marker.txt purely to prove read/write functionality post-boot — low-risk and directly tied to evidence collection. No unnecessary, unrelated, or destructive mutations were found; the lifecycle diff shows only the expected boot_id change and ephemeral systemd-private temp dirs (normal boot artifacts, not executor residue). No failed services, package-health issues, or unsafe new listening sockets appeared in the after_executor snapshot.
